new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate 'lexical' syllable, i.e. the penultimate vowel or diphthong of the phonemic representation; phonetic intrusive (epenthetic) vowels inside consonant clusters do not count (e.g. /ptou/ [pə̆.tóu̯] 'closed' is stressed on its only lexical syllable). Examples: ata [á.ta] 'cut', okur [ɔ́.kur] 'next day', lerimi [lɛ.rí.mi] 'your (pl.)', takrɨngə [ta.krɨ́ŋ.gə] 'like this', wusanapə [wu.sa.ná.pə] 'father'; multimorphemic w-mb-naki [wə̆m.bə̆.ná.ki] 'she tells me/us'. Long vowels occur only in stressed syllables. Stress is not contrastive; the author reports duration as its main correlate and calls the analysis impressionistic (no acoustic study).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned. §2.6 states that reduplicated forms (e.g. nongnongal) and CVC-reduplicated ideophones (galgal, karkar, tungtungor) carry two independent primary stresses and are therefore analysed as two phonological words.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 107: 'The only words whose stress pattern does not conform to the stress rule discussed above are a few words used in the mountain language, a special register used by hunters in the mountains, with stress on the last syllable, such as ainel [aɪ̯.nɛ́l] "bush knife" and walpuk [wal.púk] "dog".' Also: proper nouns with three-vowel sequences (Suau, Muei) are disyllabic with stress on the first /u/ (§2.1.2); word-final sequences of identical vowels behave differently from diphthongs for stress (§2.1.2); clitics never bear stress, and the particles ka (past), ma (potential) and ku 'still' are unstressed while tu, ar/aruəp, mo, kosu are stressed (§8.2-8.3).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (phonological word) stress, described on citation-form words from a lexical database of about 1,250 entries and multimorphemic verb forms; based on the author's field impressions plus some Praat checks. Phrase-level intonation is treated separately in §2.7 (declaratives falling, polar questions rising). Note: italic example words in the captured text are font-shifted; the decoded forms above are from the accompanying IPA.
new_statements.identity_note: The source describes Srenge, the speakers' own name for the language the literature calls Aruop (ISO 639-3 lsr; the dissertation itself gives 'ISO code lsr, Glottolog code aruo1240'). Aruop is the word for 'no'; Lawu Srenge = 'language Srenge'. Spoken in the 'old villages' Alona, Anipo, Marakumba, Parkop, Suwara and the 'new villages' Asier and Sibilanga (Laycock 1968/1973 list Asier, Makumba, Yinungen); about 200 speakers. Fieldwork was with consultants from Asier and Sibilanga; no dialect division is described, so the statement applies to the language as a whole.
